subChunks.title: Scalability, Load Balancing & Caching
subChunks.hookHtml: System design is where engineering judgment matures into architectural thinking. It's the skill that separates engineers who build features from engineers who build platforms. There is no single right answer — only trade-offs, and the ability to reason about them clearly.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Scalability Fundamentals

Vertical scaling (scale up): add more resources to one machine (more CPU, more RAM). Simple; has hard limits; expensive at the top end; single point of failure.

Horizontal scaling (scale out): add more machines running the same service. Unlimited in theory; requires stateless services (or externally managed state); more complex operations.

Stateless services are the prerequisite for horizontal scaling. Any instance must be able to handle any request. State must live outside the service: in a database, cache, or object store — not in memory or local disk.

Load Balancing

Distributes incoming requests across multiple service instances.

  • Round-robin: requests rotate through instances in order. Simple; works when requests are roughly equal cost.
  • Least connections: route to the instance with fewest active connections. Better for variable-cost requests.
  • Consistent hashing: same request key always routes to the same instance (useful for cache locality, stateful connections).
  • Health checks: load balancer removes unhealthy instances; adds them back after recovery. Critical for zero-downtime deployments.

Caching

Caching reduces latency and database load by serving repeated data from fast storage.

Cache aside (lazy loading): application checks cache first; on miss, loads from DB and populates cache. Most common pattern.

Write-through: on every write, update both cache and DB. Consistent but adds write latency.

Write-back (write-behind): write to cache immediately; async write to DB. Lowest write latency; risk of data loss on cache failure.

Cache invalidation: the hardest problem. Options: TTL (expiry), explicit eviction on write, event-driven invalidation.

Cache stampede: many requests hit the DB simultaneously when a popular cache entry expires. Fix: lock-based refresh (one request refreshes; others wait), staggered TTLs, pre-emptive refresh.

Database Scaling

Read replicas: primary handles writes; replicas serve reads. Replication lag means replicas may be slightly stale. Good for read-heavy workloads.

Sharding: partition data across multiple databases by a shard key (e.g. user ID). Allows horizontal DB scaling. Queries that span shards are expensive. Cross-shard transactions are very hard.

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): separate read and write models. Writes update the authoritative store; reads query a denormalised projection optimised for query patterns.

Estimating Scale

Back-of-envelope calculations are expected in system design. Useful numbers: 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 requests/second at uniform rate. A web server can handle ~10K connections. A typical DB can handle ~10K queries/second on single node. 1TB = 10^12 bytes; SSD random read ≈ 100µs; network within datacenter ≈ 0.5ms.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's spellbook lookup handled 100 requests per second reliably. When the spring tournament started, it received 10,000 per second. Nothing had been designed to scale. One server, one database, all data in memory. It collapsed in 90 seconds. Three months later, after a proper system design exercise, the same team handled a million requests per second with confidence.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Vex
storyBeats.text: System design is not about knowing the right answer. It's about asking the right questions first. How many users? Read-heavy or write-heavy? What consistency requirements? What's the latency budget? What's the failure tolerance? The answers to these questions determine the architecture — not your favourite technology.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Vex
storyBeats.text: Horizontal scaling requires stateless services. This is the constraint everything else flows from. If your service stores session state in a local hashmap, you cannot add a second instance — requests go to different instances and state is lost. The fix: externalise all state. Session in Redis. Files in object storage. Database for everything persistent.

storyBeats.speaker: Principal Engineer Vex
storyBeats.text: Cache invalidation is genuinely hard — Phil Karlton listed it as one of the two hard problems in computer science. The safest approach: use TTLs as a safety net (data goes stale at worst after N minutes), and explicitly invalidate when you know data has changed. Never rely on TTL alone for consistency-sensitive data.

Vex draws the whiteboard diagram: load balancer, three stateless app servers, Redis cache, PostgreSQL primary, two read replicas. 'This is the answer to 80% of medium-scale systems. Understand this before adding Kafka or sharding.'

learningObjectives: Distinguish vertical and horizontal scaling and explain why horizontal scaling requires stateless services
Describe cache-aside, write-through, and write-back patterns and when to use each
Explain read replicas, sharding, and CQRS as database scaling strategies
Estimate rough capacity from given requirements (requests/day → requests/second, storage estimates)
commonMistakes: Adding horizontal scaling before removing local state from services — requests fail randomly depending on which instance handles them
Caching without TTLs or invalidation — stale data served indefinitely
Sharding on a hot key (e.g. all writes for one tenant go to one shard) — uneven load defeats the purpose
Over-engineering for 10x scale when the current system needs 2x — YAGNI applies to architecture too
assessmentCriteria: Can draw a simple scalable architecture (load balancer, stateless app servers, cache, DB) and explain each component's role
Can explain the cache-aside pattern step by step, including what happens on cache miss and cache hit
Can describe three consistency trade-offs of eventual consistency in read replicas
Can do a rough back-of-envelope calculation (e.g. 10M users making 5 reads/day = requests/second)
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through designing a URL shortener (like bit.ly) from scratch. What are the requirements? Where are the bottlenecks? How would you scale to handle 100 million redirects per day? What would you cache, and why?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
System design exercise — answer in writing:

  1. You need to design a spell lookup service used by 1 million mages, each looking up 10 spells per day. (a) Calculate the requests per second at peak (assume 10× average). (b) List the three architectural components you would add to handle this scale.
  2. Your service has three stateless app servers behind a load balancer. A user logs in, gets a session token, and the next request goes to a different server. What breaks, and how do you fix it?
  3. You cache spell data with a 10-minute TTL. An admin updates a spell's damage value. How long before the cache serves the new value? How would you reduce this to near-zero latency?
  4. Explain why sharding on tier (APPRENTICE/JUNIOR/SENIOR/LEAD) is a bad shard key for an Academy-wide database.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. (a) 1M mages × 10 requests/day = 10M requests/day.
   10M / 86,400s ≈ 116 req/s average.
   10× peak = 1,160 req/s.
   (b) Three components: (1) Caching layer (Redis) to serve repeated spell lookups without DB queries;
   (2) Read replicas to distribute read load from DB; (3) CDN/static cache for spell assets if applicable.

2. The session state (stored in one server's memory) is not visible to other servers.
   When the second request hits a different server, the session is not found — the user appears logged out.
   Fix: externalise session state to a shared store (Redis, or a database-backed session). All servers read from the same session store.

3. With a 10-minute TTL, the stale value is served for up to 10 minutes.
   To reduce to near-zero: explicitly invalidate the cache key when the admin updates the spell.
   Implementation: after the DB update, call cache.delete("spell:" + spellId). The next read will fetch from DB and repopulate the cache.
   Belt-and-suspenders: keep a short TTL as a safety net even with explicit invalidation.

4. There are only 4 tier values — APPRENTICE, JUNIOR, SENIOR, LEAD. With sharding by tier:
   - Only 4 shards maximum (wasted horizontal capacity)
   - Most users are APPRENTICE or JUNIOR — highly uneven distribution (hot shards)
   - Cross-tier queries require scatter-gather across all shards
   Better shard key: user ID hash — distributes users evenly across any number of shards.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design the architecture for the Academy's real-time tournament leaderboard. Requirements: 100,000 concurrent users viewing the leaderboard during a 2-hour tournament. Leaderboard updates every second as spells are scored. Reads vastly outnumber writes (1000:1 ratio). Maximum acceptable staleness: 5 seconds.

Answer: (1) What database do you use and why? (2) What caching strategy, TTL, and invalidation approach? (3) How do you handle the write spike when thousands of spells score simultaneously? (4) Draw or describe the full architecture in words. (5) What is the single biggest risk in your design?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Database: Redis sorted set as the primary leaderboard store (ZADD for O(log N) score insert, ZRANGE for O(log N + K) range query). Back-fill to PostgreSQL for persistent audit. Redis handles the hot path.

2. Caching: The leaderboard itself is the cache (Redis sorted set). Reads serve directly from Redis. For the HTTP tier: short 1-second HTTP cache header prevents hammering Redis for every page refresh from 100K users.
   TTL: 5 seconds (matches acceptable staleness). Invalidation: writes update Redis immediately (no separate invalidation needed — Redis is the source of truth for the hot path).

3. Write spike: use an async queue (Kafka topic 'spell.scored'). Score events are written to Kafka (fast, high-throughput) and consumed by a leaderboard worker that batches ZADD operations to Redis. Rate of writes to Redis is decoupled from the spike rate.

4. Architecture:
   Clients → CDN (1s cache for top-10 static render) → Load Balancer → Stateless API servers → Redis (sorted set leaderboard) ← Leaderboard Worker ← Kafka ← Spell Scoring Service → PostgreSQL (durable audit)

5. Biggest risk: Redis single point of failure. Fix: Redis Sentinel or Redis Cluster for HA. Also: memory overflow if the leaderboard grows unboundedly — cap with ZREMRANGEBYRANK to keep top N entries only.

questions.prompt: Which condition is required before a service can be horizontally scaled (multiple identical instances)?
options: The service must use a relational database
The service must be stateless — no local session state or in-memory data that must survive between requests
The service must implement the Circuit Breaker pattern
questions.answer: The service must be stateless — no local session state or in-memory data that must survive between requests
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling sends requests to any available instance. If an instance stores state locally (in memory, local files), a request to a different instance will not have that state. Stateless services externalise all state — sessions to a shared cache, files to object storage, data to a database — so any instance can handle any request.

questions.prompt: A popular spell page is cached with a 5-minute TTL. When the spell is updated in the database, how long can users see stale data with a TTL-only invalidation strategy?
options: Immediately updated — the cache checks the DB on every read
Up to 5 minutes — until the TTL expires
Permanently — the TTL only affects new entries
Up to 10 minutes — the cache has a grace period
questions.answer: Up to 5 minutes — until the TTL expires
questions.explanation: With TTL-only invalidation, cached entries are served until they expire regardless of underlying data changes. Users may see stale data for the full TTL duration (5 minutes in this case). For lower staleness, add explicit cache invalidation (delete the cache key) when the spell is updated, and keep TTL as a safety net for cache-delete failures.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard service uses read replicas for scale. A user casts a spell and their score updates. They refresh the leaderboard and their new score is not shown. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The user is being load-balanced to a different server
Replication lag — the read replica has not yet received the write from the primary
The cache TTL has not expired yet
questions.answer: Replication lag — the read replica has not yet received the write from the primary
questions.explanation: Read replicas receive updates asynchronously from the primary, typically with milliseconds to seconds of lag. Writes go to the primary; reads may come from a replica that hasn't received the write yet. Solutions: route reads to the primary for operations that need strong consistency (e.g. 'read your own writes'), use synchronous replication for critical data, or accept the eventual consistency window.
